utterances.text: Do we need to go through the entire exercise, Mr. Di Fazio? It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: My question was designed to avoid precisely that, if Your Honours please. I'll make it clear to the witness so that he understands.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Mr. Stevanovic, what I'm asking you about is this: Just go through the list and tell us if you know of any men who back in 1992 were clearly, in your opinion anyway, clearly in their 60s or 70s. In other words, old men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Elderly men.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Elderly men. I'm sorry, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know exactly how old these men were. I know that this Pero Ilic was a youngish man, whereas these other people were sort of elderly people. Some have even died in the meantime. They're no longer with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Did you ever see action, and by that I mean military action, in company with any of the men listed here, apart from the younger man, Ilic, Pero? Did you ever --

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. Not with a single one of them, Pero included.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Now, you said that you had a work obligation in 1993 with these people. What was that work obligation?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The sowing and planting of crops in the month of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Why would you in particular have been involved in that particular sowing of crops in April of that year? Why weren't you fighting?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's easier to sleep at home than in a trench, in the soil. And to risk being killed. Everybody always made an effort to try to get away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I can well understand -- sorry. I can understand that, but how did you engineer it? How did you work things out so that you weren't sleeping in a trench and being shot at or fighting and instead were back in your village conducting the sowing and reaping?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even now I'm one of the more prominent farmers there and food producers in the area, so they let me go back to organise the spring sowing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And lastly, you were asked questions by Defence counsel regarding --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Just before you leave this document, D49, I would like to ask either the Prosecution or the Defence with regard to the translation. Now, is the English translation list of salaries of the fighters from Fakovici completely identical with the Bosnian Serbian original? Because at least the sequence of the words is different in the Bosnian than in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: It may be, if Your Honours -- what I can do is ask the witness to read it out into the transcript and get an official interpretation. That might solve the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Just read out the title slowly into --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could you please bear in mind the following: That the translation service has a lot of work to do, and therefore when lists are being translated usually they just translate the heading and then they say a list of 19 names follows. So this is the practice followed by the translation service here. They do not type out the actual list of names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you missed completely what -- the point that Judge Eser wanted to make. What we are interested in knowing is whether when we say -- when we have in the English text: "List of salaries for fighters from Fakovici," whether this is a correct translation of what we have in the original text which is "Spisak Boraca Fakovici."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely correct translation. Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could I ask you, Mr. Stevanovic, to read the title of that document in your own language, and that's everything that there is from the first word "Spisak" up to when you reach September. Don't read September, October, November. Could you read it out aloud, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] List of fighters from Fakovici in terms of salaries for September, October, November 1993 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, sir. Yes, Mr. Di Fazio, do you have any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, not on this particular document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. I meant -- you're still in re-examination; that was my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I've just about wrapped it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, it's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You were asked about your encounter with a man called Mehmed Tiro --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one intervention, please. September, October, November. It does not say "1993." It says list of fighters from Fakovici. But this is what it says in the transcript so...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are right. So with reference to page 50, line 5, where it says in terms of salaries from September, October, November 1993, the witness never mentioned 1993. And certainly the document does not purport to cover those three months for that particular year but for the previous year. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Within the heading it also says the document was drafted on the 25th of February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But that obviously means that September, October, and November that are mentioned there are September, October, and November of the previous year and not of 1993. So let's proceed. Your question, Mr. Di Fazio, was: "You were asked" or you had just started. "You were asked about your encounter with a man called Mehmed Tiro." And you were about to continue when we interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's right. Thank you, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. So you were asked about him and some questioning that he underwent. My question is very simple: Were you questioning him or asking him questions in any official capacity when you saw him in 1993, in an official capacity?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Were you in company with another soldier who was asking him some sort of questions in an official capacity?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Who was the other soldier and what was he asking?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was from the police station in Fakovici. There was this police station there, so he was from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So what was your purpose in questioning Mehmed?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He questioned him. I was present and I asked him only certain matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. What did you want to find out about from Mr. Mehmed? What was your purpose in asking him some questions?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I asked him whether he took part in the attack on my village because I did not see him during the attack. So that's why I asked him whether he took part in the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. And why did you want to ask him those questions?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, just like that, out of curiosity, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Di Fazio. Judge Brydensholt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: This questioning of Mehmed Tiro, where did it take place? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know how it was. He was wounded. It was at the clinic. There was nothing much happening. They were just talking. It was at Skelani that he was eventually interrogated and everything he said was written down. But at first nothing was written down. It was just a talk that we had. He was being administered first aid at the clinic in Fakovici and then he was transferred to Skelani. That's as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: What was the reason why you went to this clinic? Was it because you knew that he was there and you would like to get some information from him or why did you go to the clinic?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were there in Fakovici when he was brought in. We were there. It's a small village, you know. It's not a big town, so that it's not like we actually went anywhere. It was right in the middle of the village. You have the small clinic there, you have the school building. It's all a very small village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: But was it only you? You mentioned that you were together with a soldier. Was it only you and the soldier who asked him questions or did many more people or more people participate in this questioning, this visit to the clinic?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were more people and there was the nurse who dressed his wounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Judge Brydensholt. Judge Eser? No. Mr. Stevanovic, I am still a little bit perplexed in relation to the statement that you were shown earlier on which refers to the date of the 20th of December 1994. You recall that I had asked you specifically -- Madam Usher, could you please show him again this and put it on the ELMO page by page so that it can be followed. I want you -- or I would like you, sir, to go through that statement page by page, look at the bottom of each page, except the last one where your signature appears further up. I want you to confirm or I would like you to confirm to us that that is indeed your signature on each page.

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the first one. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On the last page there are two more signatures. On the left there is a signature and in a word "Zapisnicar," "Zapisnicar." Do you recognise that signature?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And do you recognise the signature of the Judge on the right?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you recall someone signing the same document on which you had affixed our own signature?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you repeat the name of the person who came to interview you at your home?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know the name was Sinisa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And earlier on you seemed to have suggested that he asked you to sign in blank a number of pages which he would then fill in. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you remember how many pages you signed?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you confirmed that when you signed these pages there was absolutely nothing else written on them or typed on them?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you remember being asked to sign one page not at the bottom but somewhere up on the page towards the middle of the page?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You had no problem in signing these pages blank?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't know there would be a trial one day. I didn't know why they wanted me to sign. If I had known why they wanted me to sign, I certainly wouldn't have signed. He gave me a pen and a paper and he said that he would transfer it from a notebook that he was using and that he would type it up on these blank sheets of paper. I never saw my own statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you know this man Sinisa from before?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did he show you any identification before he started interviewing you?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No identification whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you gave sort of a statement or you answered questions to a person who you did not know from before and who did not even identify himself to you?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that he was from Zvornik, an investigator. That was all he said, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you did not ask him to give you proof of that?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please, I am going to refer you to the last page of that statement precisely on the part that shows on the monitor at the moment which is -- which reads as follows: "That is all I have to say. The record has been read out aloud to me and it includes everything I have stated. I do not wish to read it. I acknowledge it as my own and hereby affix my signature." You were asked a question or more than one question on this part of the statement. Do you recall giving an answer? You were asked about this by Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't understand the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you recall -- do you remember that earlier on this morning Madam Vidovic asked you about this last paragraph of the statement and asked you precisely whether this was true or not?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that she did ask me that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And do you remember particularly yourself referring to the part of that statement which says: "I do not wish to read it," and you said, "How could anyone say that?" Do you remember saying so?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you perhaps explain to me how you were so surprised that anyone would make that statement, in other words: "I do not wish to read it," and yet be very complacent and very ready to sign out -- or put his signature on a blank document? How could you reconcile the two?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how those two can be reconciled, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think I don't have any further questions. Basically that means that your testimony comes to an end here. You will be escorted by Madam Usher who will accompany you. And then you will receive all the assistance you require to enable you to return home. Before you leave, however, I have a further question. I want to put my mind at rest on something. During this weekend, did you have an opportunity to discuss your testimony or the matters on which you have been testifying with anyone?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the exception of those who came to my room and took me to dinner, no. But they were not testifying. We were only talking about life in Holland and life over in Bosnia, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm referring to matters related to your testimony. Did you discuss matters on which you have been testifying with any person since last Friday when you left this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: STANISA STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So on behalf of Judge Brydensholt, Judge Eser, and on behalf of myself of course and the Tribunal I should like to thank you for coming over to give testimony. You should receive all the assistance you require to help you to facilitate your journey back home. And the final message is we all wish you a safe journey.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours, please. No problem with what Your Honours said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: It's just one issue relating to this statement. Has it been marked for identification or not? If it hasn't, if Your Honours please, I respectfully suggest it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You don't know how and when the issues relating to its creation might arise again, and I prefer it if it could be given -- if Your Honours prefer to have it fully tendered, I don't mind, but at the very least marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The Serbian -- the statement that Your Honours just asked him about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think what we need to do is we mark the original -- where is it? Can I have it back, please? Yeah, it's here. We can mark this one. Do you have a copy of it that you can make available?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do. I do have a copy. Do you want --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because if it's going to be marked we have to decide whether it's going to be a Prosecution Exhibit in the first place or whether it's going to be a Court/Trial Chamber exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm happy for it to be marked as a Prosecution Exhibit, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So let this be admitted in evidence and we'll give it the sequence number, that will be P4-0 --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 406, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 406. So that will be P406. And I suppose you have no problems because you have asked questions on it just the same? All right. Let me get the English translation. In the meantime, is there anything you wish to state in relation to the next witness before he is admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will give the floor to Ms. Joanne Richardson who joined the team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There are no -- there are no protective measures in place?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Good morning. No, there are no protective measures for this witness. I believe we've already -- there will be one exhibit that I will be using, which is a map. And I also turned over some of my notes to the Defence counsel about an hour ago, following proofing of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. What's the problem?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can I ask -- one moment. Mr. Wubben and Madam Vidovic, could you come here -- come near us a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We are going to have a very short break which is necessary for organisation purposes, and we will reconvene as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before we bring in the witness, we've wasted three-quarters of an hour plus because of this misunderstanding that seems to have happened. I understand that mistakes do happen and misunderstandings do happen. I do not intend to prolong it further or to make a mountain out of it. So I'm just saying that we hope that we will not have a repetition of this. On the other hand, before we start with this witness, I would like to know how much time you require, Madam Vidovic, or Mr. Jones, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Well, obviously, depending on the length of the examination-in-chief, I imagine an hour and a half to two hours maximum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Two hours. And your direct will last how long?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: About approximately two and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we can still make it, in other words. But as we go along since this, what happened, is through no fault of your own, as you go along if you think you will require more than an hour and a half, please draw my attention because I want to make sure that once this has happened that you will certainly have your two hours or one and a half hours as you may need, as you may require.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's very kind of Your Honour. I'm much obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's not lose more time and bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are Milenko Stevanovic, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I want to make sure first and foremost that what I am saying in English is being translated to you in your own language and that you can hear the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I welcome you to this Tribunal, and I welcome you on behalf of Judge Brydensholt, who comes from Denmark, Judge Eser, who comes from Germany, and of course on my own behalf, my name is Agius, I come from Malta, from the island of Malta. I welcome you. You are about to start giving evidence in this trial. Our Rules require that before you do so you enter -- you make a solemn declaration, something similar and equivalent to an oath. The solemn declaration states that in the course of your testimony that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text of the solemn declaration is contained on a piece of paper Madam Usher is going to hand to you. I would like to ask you to read that out aloud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us that you will be testifying the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Stevanovic. Please do take a chair. And let me explain to you what's going to happen. You are first going to be asked a series of questions by Ms. Richardson, who I suppose you have already met. She will then be followed by Mr. Jones who is appearing for Naser Oric. In accordance with the oath -- with the solemn declaration that you have just entered, may I remind you that your obligation to this Tribunal is to answer all questions truthfully and as fully as possible, irrespective of who is putting the question to you. In other words, you do not have the right to discriminate in favour of the Prosecution or against the Defence. Your duty, your responsibility, your obligation is to answer all questions, irrespective of where they are coming from, and to answer them truthfully and fully. Did I make myself clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Richardson, could I invite you to start with your direct. And with regard to the basic information, you can lead the witness straight away.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Stevanovic, can you please confirm for us that you were born on January 18th, 1965, that you are unmarried, you are of Serb ethnicity, and you are presently a construction worker residing in Skelani, but prior to this you were a farmer and lived in the hamlet of Bradjevina, village of Ratkovici, in the municipality of Srebrenica. Can you confirm this information by a verbal yes.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And in 1992 you resided in Bradjevina with your mother, father, and brothers?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Bradjevina is a purely Serb hamlet. There are approximately 12 households, and I'm referring specifically to the year of to 1992, and in 1992 prior to your leaving the hamlet, there were approximately 30 to 50 individuals living in the hamlet.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: The individuals who resided in Bradjevina in 1992, this was a -- basically an agricultural community, most of the people were farmers?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And within the hamlet of Bradjevina in 1992, there was a cemetery, there was no school, there was no police station, and there were no military facilities?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: At this time I would like to show you --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: If I could ask the usher for her assistance in handing out a map to Your Honours as well as to the Defence and to place the map on the ELMO for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I would ask that this map be given a number for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So could you give me the progressive number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it will be Exhibit number P407.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this document, this map, is being tendered and admitted into evidence as Prosecution Exhibit P407.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Stevanovic, could you please take a look at the map that's on the ELMO and could you locate the hamlet of Bradjevina and please draw a circle around it. I will -- you can draw that with the marker that I'm handing out to the usher. Please circle Bradjevina.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Witness complies].

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And also, could you locate the surrounding villages --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment because we need to see it. Okay. Could you just go over it -- once you've found it, could you go over it with the highlighter, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Witness complies].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could the technicians zoom in so we can follow. I can see it on my own map, but the public may --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Could you circle that, Bradjevina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Bradjevina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see clearly. I see it on the screen but not over here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, could you help the witness a little bit. We're talking of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Witness complies].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you find it? Yeah, okay. Could you put your initials next to that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Witness complies].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Could you tell us -- and just so we're clear, Bradjevina is a purely Serb hamlet. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Could you tell us what the ethnic make-up of the surrounding villages of Bradjevina, what is the ethnic make-up, and could you circle those villages and tell us at the same time whether these are Serb or Muslim villages or whether these villages are mixed. If you look at the map.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Ratkovici local commune only has Serb villages and all the population there was Serb. Bradjevina is part of that local commune.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Could you circle Ratkovici on the map, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Just in the interests of time, if Your Honours allow me, I would like to call out some of the villages and the witness can tell us whether they were Serb or Muslim villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Please locate the village Kaludra on the map and tell us whether this was a Serb village or a Muslim village. And please circle that village. Was this a Serb village?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Witness complies]. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Next could you find the village Vranesevici, circle it, and tell us whether this was a Serb or a Muslim village.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's also a Serb village, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And also could you locate the village Magudovici and draw a circle around it and tell us whether this was a Serb or a Muslim village.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Witness complies].

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Also could you locate the village Ducici and tell us -- circle it and tell us whether it was a Serb or a Muslim village.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: A Serb village.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Next the village of Durici. Could you circle that and tell us whether it's a Serb or a Muslim village.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: The village of Ducici, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, please. It's a Serb village?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Ducici is already marked from before.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, actually I wanted the witness to locate Dvoriste.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Dvoriste?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I may not be pronouncing it 100 per cent accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: But could you find that village, if you understand the village that I'm referring to, and tell us whether it's a Serb village or a Muslim village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Dvoriste --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And finally --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And is it the village that you meant him to indicate to us or not? Dvoriste, D-v-o-r-i-s-t-e?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And while we are at it, earlier on you asked the witness to show us the village of Magdovici. He showed one which on the map is spelled Magudovici. Is it the same one you meant or is it a different one?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: It is the same one, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's just to make sure for the record. I mean, I know it's a question of pronunciation more than anything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And finally could you locate the village of Oparci and circle it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And Judge Eser is pointing out to me whether Dvoriste was an exclusively Serbian village or whether it was a mixed or a Muslim village.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, purely Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And if you could look at the map and locate the village of Oparci and tell us -- please circle that village and tell us whether it was a purely Serb village or a Muslim village.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Witness complies].

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Could you tell us: Is this a Serb village?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And on this map could you show us where the nearest -- the closest Muslim village is located.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Shall we give him another highlighter with a different colour, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I was just about to do that. I will hand up to the usher a highlighter, a blue highlighter. I would ask the witness to locate that village.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Witness complies].

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: You have just circled a village called Mocevici. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Is this a Serb or a Muslim village?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would ask that P407, Prosecution's exhibit, be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. It is being admitted, as I said earlier, as Exhibit P407, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Just --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I would ask the usher's indulgence one more time just to show the witness the map. He will not be writing anything but to just show him the map itself. I would like to ask one last question before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One question, Ms. Richardson: Do you intend this map to be used only by this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, I would ask you, Mr. Stevanovic, to take a look at the map and tell me if it is correct that the Serb villages that you have circled are essentially located in the lower region of -- the lower-lying areas of the region.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: The village of Ducici is more or less on the same altitude where Mocevici and the other Muslim villages are. The others are lower down, so the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And the Muslim villages, are they located at a higher level, in terms of the area and the region?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The village of Mocevici, Poznanovici, Osneca [phoen]. All of the other villages in the area, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stevanovic, I would like to turn your attention to the year 1992 and ask if -- what type of relationship you had with your Muslim neighbours prior to 1992. Did you have a good relationship with them?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And did there come a time that this relationship changed?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Do you recall when that was?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the month of May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what specifically happened in the month of May to change your relationship with your Muslim neighbours?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the neighbouring village of Dvoriste, a man was bringing cattle feed to his house and he was killed there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And the man who was killed was Muslim -- was Serb, excuse me?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And do you know who killed him?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: His brother said that it was people from the Mocevici and Poznanovici, from one of those two villages, but he said they were from Mocevici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And these were Muslim villages?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did anything else happen in the month of May that contributed to the change of the relationship?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In Srebrenica on the 8th of May, Goran Zekic, a member of parliament, got killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And do you know how and by whom?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: He was ambushed in Potocari as he was going from Srebrenica to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And do you know who ambushed him?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: People said that -- said at that time that it was some kind of Muslim extremists, whatever. Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And did anything else, other than the killing of these two individuals, that changed your relationship with your Muslim neighbours?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In Zeleni Jadar something happened there, too. There was an ambush and an entire family got killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did there also come a time that there was no electricity in your village?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And do you know why this was?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: The transmission line that brought electricity to us went from Sase, through Skenderovici,, Mocevici, and went down to our villages. And the transmission lines were cut somewhere on their territory, in their villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: When you say "their," are you talking about the Muslim villages?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, I would like to bring your attention to May of 1992. Did anything in particular happen in your -- in any of the neighbouring villages?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Towards the end of May, the village of Oparci was torched.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And could you tell us what you know of -- when you say "torched," what do you mean? By whom?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I mean it was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And who destroyed the village?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, what can you tell us about the destruction of this village? Were you -- is this something that you observed?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what can you tell us about the destruction of the village?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: The man got killed -- Slavko Petrovic got killed on the outskirts of the village. And his wife, Mrs. Leposila [phoen] Petrovic, was with him. And she came to our village and cried and said what happened, that her husband was killed, and that the village was burned down. We tried to get closer to the village, and we tried to get into the village in order to get the dead bodies out, but it was impossible to do so because the Muslims had already taken the entire village. And there were just ashes everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, when you say "the Muslims," are you talking -- if you could tell us specifically which Muslims are you referring to. Were they civilian Muslims or were they soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to bring your attention to June of 1992. Did anything in particular happen in any of your neighbouring villages?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 21st of June, they attacked the local commune of Ratkovici. It was again the Muslims who attacked.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: When you say "Muslims," were they civilians or soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Soldiers did it for the most part, but civilians also participated in all of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And is this information that you observed or were you told this by someone?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I watched the villages burning. I watched them from my village.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And were you able to see soldiers and civilians, or this was something you learned from other people who were present during the attack?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I saw civilians and soldiers taking away the cattle of these people, taking them out of the sheds and wherever they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And where were you when you observed them taking the livestock away?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I was in my village around my house.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And from where you were, you had -- you were able to see this occurring?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's about three or 400 metres to the other side of the river as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And could you describe for us what the soldiers were wearing. They were in uniform?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I could not tell what kind of uniforms they were, but they had all kinds of uniforms, green, black, camouflage, multi-coloured ones, all sorts of uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And other than the livestock, did you see them carrying anything else? When I say "them," the soldiers or the civilians.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: From that distance I could not see these villages. I only saw flames and ashes from that distance. But where the sheds were in the meadows, where people keep their cattle, these where I saw this, towards Poznanovici and partly towards Mocevici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: You said you saw the houses burning. Do you know the extent of damage to the houses that were burned in Ratkovici in June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the village of Ratkovici I could not see the village as a village, but I could see the hamlet of Gornji Ratkovici and Polimci and part of Dvoriste.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you later go to Ratkovici following the attack?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. I would like to direct your attention to your own village, Bradjevina, and ask you to tell us who resided in the village in June of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean -- you mean the entire population of the village or what?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes. Specifically -- I'll clarify that question. In June of 1992 did the 30 to 40 people that we -- that you confirmed earlier who had resided there in 1992, were they still there or were those numbers reduced?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was a smaller number.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: There were about 15 of us, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Were they men or women?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Three women and the rest were men.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: What happened to the other people in the village, the other women, and I imagine there were children as well, where did they go?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: After the attack against Ratkovici, we did not expect anything but a further attack on Bradjevina and Mjenice [phoen]. So we took all the people who were infirm out of the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did there come a point that Bradjevina established a village guard?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And when was this?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: May. When that man Milisav Milanovic who got killed got killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: How many people were part of this village guard?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: There were 12 of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: What were their ages?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mostly young people between the ages of 18 and 45, 50, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you -- did the village guards have uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did the village guard have any weapons?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Could you tell us what type of weapons and how many.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: We had two weapons only, an M-48 and a Russian manufactured Smajser.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And where did this weapons come from; do you know?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: These weapons were bought for money.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: From whom and by whom?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: My brother went to Fakovici and I don't know who he bought it from.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And which weapon did he buy?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: A Russian Smajser or an automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And the other weapon, do you know how that was purchased?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, the two weapons that you described, were these the weapons that the village guard would use during 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And maybe you can tell us a little bit about the village guard. What type of -- could you describe for us their duties.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: The duty of this guard was that we should be vigilant in order to inform people in a timely fashion about any possible attacks.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: When you say "inform people," how would you go about doing that if there was an attack? What did you discuss among yourselves?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is what we had worked out. If anything should happen, three bullets should be fired.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And where did you patrol? Where did the village guard patrol?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Above the village. We had three shelters where we stood guard.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And at any given time, how many people would stand guard? And could you tell us what time of day this would take place?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: During the day, we were not on guard duty. We were engaged in agriculture. We stood guard only during the night.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And were any of the men in the village guard a part of the VRS military or the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And in June of 1992, were any of the men in the village guard mobilised by Serb -- by the Serb military?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Until the attack took place, no. I mean before the 28th of June; that's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And did the village guard receive any assistance from the Serb military by way of uniforms, weapons, training?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And as far as you know, were there any Serb military forces operating in the neighbouring villages?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Are you a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: When did you become a member?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: When the party was founded. I think it was in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And have you voted and paid military dues?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. There weren't any military dues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because you said military dues --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Military dues.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suppose you were --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Obviously not military dues.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: But were there any membership fees?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And did you actually vote as a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And when was this?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the very beginning when the party was established. And after the Dayton Agreement, too. These parties are still on the voting tickets and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. I will take you now to the attack on your village, June 26th, 1992. Do you recall that day?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was the 27th of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what were you doing that day?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I was at home. I took the cattle out, or rather the oxen and the cow.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And could you tell us what happened. What did you see and hear?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: When I took the cattle out and when I tied them down in the meadow so that they could graze, about an hour after that - it was about 12.00 during the day - two or three detonations could be heard.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Could you also hear shooting?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was shooting, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what happened next?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: At that moment I thought that we were probably attacked. And I went home.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: You went to your house?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And why did you do that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's where my brother was and both my parents, my father and mother.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And did you get to your home?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. Not quite. I met my brother on the way, so I went to the house later to see my parents.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Could you tell who was doing the shooting and who was responsible for this explosion?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And who was that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Muslim army who reached the house and were at a distance of about 100 metres from the house itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And how were the soldiers dressed? Could you see?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I could.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Could you tell us what uniforms they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: They wore camouflage green uniforms, forest keepers uniforms that were green. There were black uniforms there. They had black and green caps on their heads.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And were they saying anything that you could hear at that point?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what did you hear them saying?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: The loudest thing was Allahu Akbar or whatever they say.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: What does that mean as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we all know what it means.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: What else did they say?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: They cursed our Serbian mother. They shouted things like: Catch them alive or give them to us so we can cut their throats.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And where were you when you were able to hear these remarks being made?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: At that time I was not far from the house, perhaps 100 metres from the house, in the bush because there is a creek running by the house.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Can you tell us when you got back to your house what happened. I'm not sure, did you actually get back to your house? I think you said no.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Were there other members of your family in the village at the time of the attack?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And who were they?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: One of my brothers.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: What about your parents?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: They were with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And how many soldiers were you able to see from where you were?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: In my yard and around the stable I think about 30 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And approximately how many soldiers do you think were in the village that day?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: The village itself is about 300 or 400 metres across. From the place of their attack, I think there were about 500 of them, certainly not less.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Was there any member, including yourself, were any members of the village guard shooting at the soldiers from what you could see?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what did you see the soldiers doing? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: From my position, I couldn't see the village. I only saw my own yard and the house and what they were doing around the house.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. Well, tell us about that. What could you see them doing in your own yard and to your own house?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: They were taking things out of my house. They were killing my pigs in the yard.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: What type of things were they taking?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: All the household appliances, starting with the bed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Anything else?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: The freezer, the electrical oven, the electrical heater. I had a mill also, a TV, a radio.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And after the soldiers removed these items -- I'm sorry, were you completed -- did you complete the list of things you saw them taking or did you need to continue?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Then they torched the house and the stable.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: How did you torch the house? Were you able to see?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: First you could hear two explosive devices and then I saw smoke rising from the house and the stable. Later there was a flame and the whole thing just tumbled down.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Let's go to the stable. Were you able to see the stable from where you were?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what did you see them doing, the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I had a young calf in the stable. The calf was screaming, and in that -- it was caught inside the flame and I saw the stable burning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And did they remove anything from the stable, any of your livestock?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. Not from the stable. There was this calf that was burning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: You mentioned the pigs earlier. What did you see them doing to the pigs?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I saw that they were killing them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: How?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: They were using automatic weapons. The pigs were outside in the yard, and they were killing them all over the place.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Were you able to observe what they did with the household items they removed from your house?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, nothing further that I could see.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, after the soldiers burned your house and exploded -- released this explosion, did you see anyone else after the soldiers come into your village and remove anything from -- or I should say anyone else coming into the village?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Civilians came, Muslims. They came after the military.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: These civilians, were they men or women?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: All kinds, both men and women.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: How do you know they were Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: They kept shouting Allahu Akbar, and they kept yelling: Catch those Serbs alive. They put SDS [as interpreted] symbols and signs on the walls of the houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: SDS symbols or SDA symbols?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: SDA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: What else did you see them doing? Were they removing any property or transporting any of the items away?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I was not able to see anything else that they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, while you were -- well, let me do this. I would like to show you, with the usher's assistance, Prosecution's Exhibit 407, the map that you used earlier. I would like you to take a look at that map and could you tell us and draw on the map -- I would hand up a pen to the usher, a red pen --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: With Your Honours' permission. We just need another colour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Can you tell us which direction you first heard the shooting coming from when the village was under attack. If you can look at the map and draw with an arrow or arrows from what direction you heard the shooting and explosion.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean my village?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, first locate your village --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think -- let me can help a little bit. I think we should focus the camera on Bradjevina, where Bradjevina is and then zoom -- put that in the centre of the monitor, of the screen. Bring it -- yes, exactly. And this should help the witness indicate better. You can look at the monitor before you mark. That's Bradjevina. And we would like to know from which direction you heard the shooting coming from.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Witness complies].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you need to explain that a little bit. For the record, the witness draws a circular line which, however, does not become a complete circle around Bradjevina. And then to the left of the unfinished part of that would-be circle he draws a vertical line starting from the number 651 on the map -- on the map. Yes. Could you explain what you indicated on that map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were entirely surrounded from all sides. There were attacks. And the first shots were fired from the direction of Kaludra, below the village. And then after that, the shooting spread on all sides between Vranesevici, Magudovici, Bradjevina. And I didn't shut the roof because there was an attack coming from the village. There was an elevation up there that they had seized control of.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Could you --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Ms. Richardson, he's your witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: If you could assist us further and draw an arrow from Kaludra from where you heard the shots being fired. We understand that the circle means that it spread and it was coming from all over at a certain point, but you just mentioned the village Kaludra. Could you draw an arrow and point so that the record is clear.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Witness complies].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And were these artillery shots, small weapons, rifles, or were they mortars or what were they, the shots that you heard coming from the direction of Kaludra? Could you describe them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The shooting was just below the village. That was from the direction of Kaludra. I'm talking about the side that the shooting came from. And the detonations that we could hear inside the village, I think those were bombs, explosive devices. I don't think they had any artillery weapons or heavy weaponry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We can put the map away for now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Could you tell us -- you stated that you were in the bushes and could you tell us who you were with.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: My brother was there, my mother and my father. Later some other people from the village came over.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: When you say "came over," well, how did they -- were they trying to escape the attack? Is that why they were there?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were trying to escape from the attack. They were running from the village to the creek because that was the only shelter in sight. That was a way out for us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And this creek that you were hiding by, could you tell us after you saw the -- your house -- the explosion from your house and the goods being taken out and you saw the civilians, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: At that point in time I started walking down the creek. I tried to get as far as I could so I couldn't be caught. While they were busy doing all that over there, I seized the opportunity to walk part of the way where I was most afraid they would be waiting for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you were walking along with your parents and your brother and other members of the village?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Where did you go along this creek? Where did you end up? Where did you end up?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: We walked down the river towards Grabovacka Rijeka. There's a river running between all these Serbian villages that runs towards the Drina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And were you able to see anything else as you were along this path by the stream?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I went down the stream.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what else were you able to see, if anything, with respect to the village of Bradjevina itself or any of the surrounding villages?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I walked perhaps 200 metres down the stream and then there was another path there you had to cross to get any further down. We paused there in the creek for about half an hour. There was no way to move on. They were torching stables and burning livestock. They would have noticed us. I heard sounds of crying. There was a man moaning and then crying for help.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Let me just stop you for a moment. You said they were torching stables and burning livestock. Who are you specifically referring to? Who is "they"?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And were they soldiers or civilians?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: All of them together.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So they were intermingled?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what village or hamlet were you able to see the stables being torched and the livestock being burned? Were they -- was this in Bradjevina or some other village as you were walking along the stream?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Between Bradjevina and Magudovici there are meadows belonging to people from both villages. There are meadows there jointly owned by people from both villages. That's near the creek.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. And after you passed -- as you were walking along, could you tell us what happened then. You were along the stream and then you observed the burning of the barns. What happened next?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I heard one of the Muslims yelling, calling on others.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: What was he saying?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: He was calling on Seval [phoen] from Mocevici. And he said: Seval, come on, come on, faster, faster.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you said -- did he say anything else?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I heard another man who saw Ljubisa Gajic somewhere along the road from the neighbouring village of Magudovici and he was moving towards Bradjevina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Was this the person --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Because I am sure going back to line 5 and then 6. He said: "I heard one of the Muslims yelling, calling on others." And then you reported as having asked the question what was he saying. But I recall you asking him also who was he.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And if Your Honours please, I think he also said: Come on, faster, faster.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. But let's start from this and go through this part again. This person who you heard, this Muslim yelling, calling on others and calling on Seval, do you know who he was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably one of their commanders who took part in this. I don't know because I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What was he saying, telling Seval, that you heard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was yelling at him to come faster from the river, the same direction I was headed, to the right of myself. This Ljubisa was somewhere along the road and he was calling him from up there to hurry up, to get out of the river, to cut across the path between Drajuvina [phoen] and Magudovici as fast as he could. That's at least what I thought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And Ms. Richardson, we've got one minute left. If you can conclude on this, you conclude; if not, we'll adjourn until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think I can ask one final question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: You indicated that you heard someone crying. Do you know who that was? Could you tell who was crying and where the crying was coming from?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: From my right-hand side. And the person crying was Ljubisa Gajic, not far from me. Perhaps 100 metres from where I was standing.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think we can conclude at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stevanovic, we have to stop here for today. We will continue and finish with you tomorrow, starting at 9.00. So you will be attended to. May I remind you of something very important. It's very important that you do not talk to anyone on the subject matter of your testimony. You have an absolute duty to refrain from doing so. And if anyone tries to approach you to discuss these matters, you are also duty-bound to inform us straight away.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thanks. So you will be escorted out of the courtroom. And we will adjourn. Tomorrow 9.00. I think it's in the morning again, no? Tomorrow, 9.00, and I think it's in this same courtroom. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 2nd day of November, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: [Trial Chamber and Prosecution and Defence Counsel confer]
--- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.47 p.m.,
